blocks.text:
John 1 raises several closely connected interpretive questions. In verse 1, the Greek wording distinguishes the Logos, or Word, from God—“the Word was with God”—while also predicating theos of the Word—“the Word was God.” That grammatical pattern is important for translation and interpretation, but the sentence should be read with the whole prologue rather than treated as a stand-alone formula. The prologue also has an early textual variation in verse 18: manuscripts preserve readings such as “unique God” and “unique Son.” Either reading belongs to the passage’s portrayal of Jesus as the one who makes God known.

John the Baptist’s repeated denials make clear that he is a witness rather than the Christ. His title for Jesus, “the Lamb of God,” can call to mind more than one stream of imagery, including sacrifice, Passover, servant, and apocalyptic imagery, so the chapter does not require reducing the phrase to a single association. Across verses 1–18, the Logos is presented as with God in the beginning, active in creation and life, and then becoming flesh and dwelling among human beings. Jewish Scripture, wisdom and divine-word traditions, and Greek discourse all inform how readers have understood this language.
